clinicalPearls: A serious neonatal gastrointestinal emergency of bowel inflammation and necrosis, predominantly affecting preterm infants
Presents with feed intolerance, abdominal distension, bloody stools, bilious aspirates and systemic instability
Prematurity and formula feeding increase risk, while human breast milk is protective
The abdominal radiograph may show pneumatosis intestinalis, and portal venous gas or free air indicate advanced disease
The modified Bell staging system grades severity from suspected disease to established and advanced perforation
Management ranges from bowel rest, gastric decompression and antibiotics to surgery for perforation or deterioration
reference.pathophysiology: Necrotising enterocolitis is a multifactorial disorder in which immaturity of the preterm gut, in combination with enteral feeding, an abnormal microbial colonisation pattern and mucosal ischaemia, triggers an exaggerated inflammatory response and breakdown of the intestinal barrier. Bacterial translocation across the compromised mucosa amplifies inflammation, leading to variable bowel-wall necrosis, gas within the bowel wall (pneumatosis) and, in severe cases, full-thickness necrosis with perforation and peritonitis. Although bacteria contribute, it is regarded as a distinct inflammatory-ischaemic disease of the immature gut rather than a simple infection.
additionalDifferentials: Anal fissure or swallowed maternal blood (for bloody stool)
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal radiographs for pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas and free air
Full blood count, inflammatory markers and blood culture
Blood gas, glucose and coagulation studies
Serial abdominal examination and, where used, abdominal ultrasound
Surgical review for advanced or deteriorating disease
redFlags: Rapid clinical deterioration with shock or disseminated intravascular coagulation
Abdominal wall erythema or a fixed mass
Portal venous gas or extensive pneumatosis
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies with severity; medical disease often resolves, but advanced disease carries significant mortality and long-term risks including short bowel syndrome, strictures and neurodevelopmental impairment.
pitfalls: Continuing feeds despite early warning signs
Missing perforation by not repeating imaging in a deteriorating baby
Confusing spontaneous intestinal perforation with necrotising enterocolitis
Underestimating the risk of later strictures after recovery
management: Bowel rest with cessation of enteral feeds and nasogastric decompression
Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering enteric organisms, with parenteral nutrition to maintain intake
Supportive care correcting acidosis, coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia, with fluid resuscitation, inotropes and ventilation for shock
Serial abdominal radiographs and examination to detect progression to portal venous gas or free air
Surgical intervention with laparotomy or peritoneal drainage for perforation or full-thickness necrosis
Prioritisation of human breast milk as protective, with cautious graded reintroduction of feeds on recovery
Paediatric surgical referral and long-term follow-up for strictures, short bowel syndrome and neurodevelopmental outcome
